title.narrative: UNCDF: Remittances for Development phase II
UNCDF: Remittances for Development phase II

description.narrative: Remittance for Development II is a continuation of the Remittance for Development I that Sida, has supported since 2019. The aim of the program is to strengthen the capacity of the regulator to monitor accurate and meaningful data on remittances for evidence-based policy making; developing digital channels at the regional level for migrants to send and receive remittances with the capacity to link remittances with financial products designed to their needs. The program will be conducted through the following four workstreams: 1) Enabling Policy and Regulations, 2) Open Digital Payment Ecosystems, 3) Inclusive Innovation and 4) Empowered Customers. The program is being managed through the regional hubs hosted at Regional Economic Communities and Commissions (RECs) – ECCAS (based out of Gabon), ECOWAS (for WAEMU, based out of Senegal), IGAD (based out of Djbouti), and in addition senior staff and technical capacity to be hosted in Kenya, closer to African Institute of Remittances (AIR) and AfricaNenda HQ.

Remittance for Development II är en fortsättning på ett program avseende remitteringar som Sida stödde 2019–2022. Syftet med programmet är att stärka tillsynsmyndigheters kapacitet att övervaka och samla in korrekt och meningsfulla data om remitteringar för ett faktabaserat policyutvecklande; utveckla digitala kanaler för migranter att skicka och ta emot remitteringar med kapacitet att länka remitteringar med finansiella produkter utformade för deras behov. Programmet kommer att genomföras genom följande fyra arbetsflöden: 1) stödjande policys och regleringar, 2) ett tillgängligt ekosystem för digitala betalningssystem, 3) inkluderade och innovation och 4) stärkande av kunderna. Programmet hanteras genom de regionala hubbarna hos de Regional Economic Communities (RECs) – ECCAS (baserat i Gabon), ECOWAS (för WAEMU, baserat i Senegal), IGAD (baserat i Djbouti), och därutöver teknisk expertis baserad i Kenya, närmare African Institute of Remittances (AIR) och AfricaNenda HQ.

The Goal of the Programme is to contribute to regional harmonization of remittance policies and availability of affordable, accessible, reliable, and tailored digital remittances and financial products to female and male migrants towards their economic inclusion, financial resilience, and reduced inequality.
Expected results of the Programme are as follows: 1. Regional Stakeholders: - Building on existing projects and engagements on migration and development, provided technical assistance and advocacy to the Secretariat of Regional Economic Communities (RECs) towards harmonization of mobilization of remittances flows. - Supporting RECs with the implementation of regional harmonization through the National Working Group on Remittance (NWG-R) in each Member State under the existing National Coordination Mechanism on Migration and Regional Steering Committee on Remittance (RSC-R). - Collaborate with regional technical institutions AfricaNenda, Pan Africa Payments and Settlements Systems (PAPPS), AU Statistics Commission and African Institute of Remittances with an aim to strengthen its regional and country capacity on remittance data and statistics, enabling laws and regulations and open digital payment ecosystem.
2.National Policy makers and Regulators: - Strengthened data capacity of the regulator to monitor accurate and meaningful data on remittances for evidence-based policy making. - Contribution towards regional harmonization of risk-based remittance policies and regulations. - Promotion and development of digital channels for migrants to send and receive remittances at cheaper transaction costs, improving the agent network and access points, and designing and testing migrant-centric and gender-smart financial products linked to remittances.

title.narrative: Beslut om insats Remitteringar för Utveckling II

description.narrative:
Policy and Regulatory Advancements
UNCDF conducted policy diagnostics in 44 countries and supported regional harmonization efforts within IGAD(Intergovernmental Authority on Development), ECCAS(Economic Community of Central African States), and WAEMU(West African Economic and Monetary Union). A key achievement was the integration of gender-responsive policies, ensuring that migrants and women were included in national and regional financial inclusion strategies such as in the BCEAO's(Central Bank of WAEMU) 2024 Strategy. These efforts laid the groundwork for more inclusive financial ecosystems and enabled member states to enact seven new policy and regulatory reforms, including Ethiopia's banking liberalization and Somalia's AML/CFT (Anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism) revision.
Digital Payment Ecosystem Development
The programme played a pivotal role in enabling South Sudan's first National Instant Payment System, in partnership with AfricaNADA( a non-profit organization that supports the development of inclusive instant Payment Systems across Africa). It also supported the expansion of intra-African digital remittance solutions, such as TerraPay and DTB(Diamond Trust Bank) Uganda, and introduced the Proxy Addressing System Service (PASS) which simplifies and secures cross-border payments. These innovations made remittances faster, safer, and more affordable for underserved populations.
Inclusive Innovation
In 2024, due to the postponement and cancellation of funding for Phase II by SDC, this area could not be sustained. Expansion or continuation of activities has not been possible and was on hold in Q2 2024. In the annual report and KPI, there is no clear explanation or measure being taken. However, for 2025 KPI, it was suggested that the workstream should be closed. This recommendation was based on the Mid-Term Evaluation, the departure of key staff from the Migration Money Programme, and the Withdrawal of SDC.
Strategic Engagements and Knowledge Sharing
UNCDF facilitated 17 workshops and 11 additional engagements with central banks and regional bodies. These included sessions with IGAD member states on migration data, ECCAS on remittance policy harmonization, and BCEAO on financial inclusion and data automation. Two sessions were dedicated to disseminating impact evaluation findings.
In terms of Knowledge products, 10 publications were released, including the flagship Gender Synthesis Report, a regional policy diagnostic for WAEMU, technical papers on digital ID, AML/CFT, and cross-boarder payment systems, and a Risk Management Dashboard covering 54 African countries.
Key achievements from Cross-Border Remittance Initiatives
1. Partnership-driven innovation: Collaboration with MasterCard, Equity Bank, TerraPay, and DTB Uganda expanded access to digital remittances by making financial services faster, more affordable, and more inclusive. Notable collaboration included Mastercard and Equity Bank, which enabled seamless transfers from Kenya to 30 countries; TerraPay and Diamond Trust Bank (DTB)Uganda, which launched the first intra-African digital remittance corridor between Kenya and Uganda; and UNCDF's facilitation of partnership between AfricanNenda and the Bank of South Sudan, resulting in the launch of the country's first National Instant Payment System. These initiatives addressed infrastructure gaps, promoted innovation, and aligned with broader regional integration efforts, ultimately improving service delivery and financial inclusion.
2. Role of Regional Economic Communities (RECs): Tailored engagement with IGAD, ECCAS, and WAEMU improved coordination and avoided duplication. RECs are crucial for harmonizing regional policies, though the operate differently, IGAD uses centralized coordination, ECCAS promotes country-level engagement, and WAEMU relies on its regional central bank. Understanding these roles has improved project implementation and Policy alignment. UNCDF's work with IGAD stands out as a strong model for institutionalized harmonization. Engaging REC's avoids duplication and ensures inclusive participation in remittance related initiatives.
3. Impact of political instability: Conflicts in Sudan, Rwanda, the DRC, and Burundi disrupted progress, but UNCDF maintained engagement. Political tensions in some of the member states affected the implementation of regional harmonization efforts. The conflict in Sudan severely hampered UNCDF's communication and work with the central bank, as most officials who had previously been active were unresponsive. Likewise, the escalating tension between Rwanda, the DRC, and Burundi also put a strain on working relationships. Despite these challenges, ongoing efforts by RECs and development partners aim to mitigate impacts, and UNCDF continues to engage proactively to maintain progress.
4. The different levels of development amongst the member states affect the pace at which regional harmonization is achieved: some countries lack the infrastructure to support digital remittances and faced weak legal and regulator frameworks. Also, some central banks require more capacity building support to ensure that they are able to effectively implement the policies critical for maintaining financial stability and mitigating systemic risks. For example, in IGAD, Kenya is advanced in its digital payment system, while South Sudan is still setting up its framework for remittance policy harmonization. Despite these disparities, regional harmonization provides opportunities for mutual learning and peer exchange, learning best practices, and generating convening power for collective progress.
5. Central banks have multiple competing priorities, underscoring the importance of appointing a Single Point of Contact (SPOC) to manage daily implementation activities effectively. Initial attempts at broader departmental involvement were less effective, but endorsement from IGAD Central Bank Governors facilitated dedicated SPOC appointments, ensuring clear accountability and ownership of the harmonization process.
6. Private Sector Engagement: Involving remittance Service Providers ensured inclusive service delivery and policy adoption. Engagement of private sector stakeholders, particularly Remittance Service Providers (RSPs), is essential for the successful implementation of the harmonization agenda. The RSPs, both bank and non-bank , are the ultimate target group for most of the policies and reforms being formulated. Therefore, engaging them to understand what challenges they encounter and seeking their input into proposed legal and regulatory frameworks ensures that the policies or reforms do not meet resistance. In addition, having a variety of RSPs allows for the remittance customers to have a variety of financial products and services such as savings accounts, insurance, and investment opportunities, further enhancing the public policy case for the delivery of digital remittances.
7. Gender Responsive Policies: Addressing the unique needs of migrant women through sex-disaggregated data, financial education, and consumer protection proved essential: Policymakers should engage migrants in financial inclusion strategies, leverage sex-disaggregated data, strengthen consumer protections, and promote gender sensitive financial education. UNCDF's ongoing work with BCEAO exemplifies this approach, ensuring migrants and women are central to regional financial inclusion strategies.
The three major implementation challenges and risks UNCDF faced in 2024 were:
1. Funding Uncertainty: SDC delayed its decision on Phase II funding, causing prolonged uncertainty and leading to the loss of 28 staff, including the programme manager.
2. Programme disruption: The programme experienced significant disruptions, particularly in Asia, affecting key activities related to inclusive innovation and digital payment ecosystem development. Although these challenges were regionally concentrated, they had indirect but substantial impacts on Africa. The loss of shared staff and programme leadership, delays in innovation workstreams, and reduced cross-regional collaboration slowed the pace and limited the scope of implementation in Africa.
3. Operational limitations: As a solidarity measure, travel and in-person workshops were suspended, impacting engagement with regional bodies like ECCAS and IGAD.
In conclusion, UNCDF Migration Programme in 2024 demonstrated strong progress toward building inclusive, secure, and accessible remittance systems across Least Developed Countries. Despite funding cancellation and operational challenges, the programme achieved key milestones in policy reforms, digital innovation, and gender responsive financial inclusion. Strategic partnerships and regional collaboration helped overcome barriers, while lessons learned highlighted the importance of tailored engagement, private sector involvement, and addressing political and infrastructure gaps. These efforts have laid a solid foundation for continued impact and regional harmonization in the years ahead.
